t.12.1: Janaka said: First I became intolerant of bodily action, then of extensive speech, and then of thought itself; therefore I abide just thus.
t.12.2: Since there is no delight in sound and the other sense objects, and since the Self is not an object of perception, my heart is free from both distraction and one-pointedness, and thus indeed do I abide.
t.12.4: Since there is nothing for me to reject or to accept, and likewise no joy or sorrow, now, O Brahman, I abide just thus.
t.12.3: For those distracted by notions of sameness, superimposition and the like, practice is undertaken for the sake of samādhi; having seen this rule thus, I abide just so.
t.12.5: Seeing that the stages of life and freedom from them, meditation, and the renunciation of what the mind has embraced only stir up mental distraction in me, I remain established just as I am.
t.12.6: Just as the performance of action springs from ignorance, so too does its cessation. Having rightly understood this truth, I abide just as I am.
t.12.8: He by whom this has been done in just this way, he indeed attains the fulfillment of life's purpose; he whose very nature is just thus, he indeed attains the fulfillment of life's purpose.
t.12.7: Even while contemplating the Unthinkable, one still takes on a form of thought. Therefore, having abandoned that meditation, I abide just as I am.
